notes: \cpara{States the view the post answers. The view is real. In \textsc{Kitzmiller v. Dover} (2005) a federal court ruled that Intelligent Design is not science, first because it ``violates the centuries-old ground rules of science by invoking and permitting supernatural causation.''}

\cpara{Asks whether the view means that creationism could be true and still be barred from science class. The Dover ruling's wording fits this reading: ``while ID arguments may be true, a proposition on which the Court takes no position, ID is not science.''}

\cpara{Gives a motive for the view, introduced with ``It seems clear enough'' and supported by no evidence. Other reasons are on record. One is legal: in the United States the Constitution ``does not bar the teaching of false science. It bars the teaching of non-science, especially non-science which is religion by another name'' (\textsc{Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy}, ``Creationism''). Another concerns method: the Dover court agreed with the biologist Kenneth Miller that attributing unsolved problems to causes outside the natural world is a ``science stopper.''}
\clogic{The Dover ruling did discuss this. Its third ground, any one of the three being ``sufficient,'' was that ``ID's negative attacks on evolution have been refuted by the scientific community.''}

\cpara{Says that excluding Intelligent Design a priori would make the creationists' complaint justified. The point had been made before, which supports it. After the 1982 Arkansas ruling on creation science, Larry Laudan and other philosophers objected to excluding creationism by a test of falsifiability; they ``thought Creationism false'' (\textsc{Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy}, ``Creationism'').}
\cpara{Restates the view in the voice of someone who holds it.}
\cpara{Asks what ``supernatural'' means, with a joke about a surname.}

\clogic{The post does not report what the people it answers mean by the word. Carrier, whose definition it adopts next, does: ``There is a trend in science and law to define the word `supernatural' as `the untestable','' a definition Carrier calls ``deeply flawed.'' The Dover ruling speaks in those terms, of ``an untestable supernatural force.'' On that meaning the rule excludes untestable claims, which is not a verdict on whether they are true. The post argues against the rule read with Carrier's definition, and does not take it up as read with theirs.}

\cpara{Adopts Richard Carrier's definition and credits Carrier by name. It matches Carrier's post of January 2007 in substance: ```supernaturalism' means that at least some mental things cannot be reduced to nonmental things.'' The phrase ``ontologically basic'' is the author's. ``Uncritical Supercriticality'' used this definition earlier without naming Carrier; the notes on that post give the source.}
\cpara{Illustrates the definition: water that wants to go downhill against equations of motion, a tree spirit against plant biochemistry.}

\cpara{Refers the reader to Carrier for the argument, and gives the dryad: a tree spirit found to be made of ordinary particles would no longer be supernatural. ``The dull catalogue of common things'' is Keats's phrase, from \textsc{Lamia}, taken up in ``Joy in the Merely Real.''}
\cpara{States the dilemma: fairness to religious claims against good grounds for excluding the supernatural a priori.}
\cpara{Asks what a universe would look like if reductionism were false.}

\cpara{Restates the thesis of ``Reductionism'' with a new example, the equations of Newton and Einstein for gravity as two maps of one territory. The substance matches that post's statement that ``there is only the most basic level.''}
\cpara{Begins a supposition in three short steps: the Mind Projection Fallacy true, a 747 with an existence apart from its quarks.}
\cpara{Asks what observations such a universe would produce.}
\cpara{Argues that if no observation can be named, non-reductionism is ruled out by incoherence, not by evidence.}

\clogic{Philosophers of emergence have named one. If there were strongly emergent forces or laws, ``we might expect to see, in candidate emergentist contexts, evidence for a hitherto unrecognized configurational interaction, much as occurred with the weak nuclear interaction'' (\textsc{Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy}, ``Emergent Properties''). Brian McLaughlin (1992), as the entry reports, found ``not a scintilla of evidence'' for such novelty. That is a verdict from observation, the kind the post asks for. The notes on ``The Futility of Emergence'' give C.~D. Broad's earlier form of the view.}

\cpara{States, as the author's own thesis, that non-reductionism is a confusion, and supports it with questions. The main question, why a fully specified multi-level model would not ``flatten out'' into another list of fundamental things, is what philosophers call the ``collapse'' objection to strong emergence (O'Connor 1994, Kim 1998, as the same entry reports). Defenders of emergence have replied to it; the post gives its side as a thesis and does not take up the replies.}
\cpara{Places supernaturalism inside non-reductionism, and religion inside supernaturalism.}

\cpara{Says a powerful being made of parts would be a naturalistic hypothesis, fit for a science class. Carrier's article draws the same line with a Stoic god, whose thoughts would be ``the product of a machine of some sort, like a brain.''}

\cpara{Says natural selection was not hailed as the Creator because it was not fundamentally mental. The notes on ``An Alien God'' made this point in believers' favour, against that post's charge; here the post states it itself. It fits the record. Some churchmen took the theory up at once as God's method, not as God: Darwin quoted Charles Kingsley from the second edition of the \textsc{Origin} on, that it is ``just as noble a conception of the Deity'' to believe in original forms ``capable of self-development.''}
\cpara{The dilemma: if physics and the brain are as usually understood, a brain made of quarks can only envision and predict what quarks can.}
\cpara{Concludes that people in reductionist universes can pronounce ``non-reductionist'' but cannot imagine it.}
\cpara{Explains why supernatural explanations sound simple: the brain uses its own wanting as a black box, the point of ``Occam's Razor.''}
\cpara{Gives God and the flowers: our sense of beauty is opaque to us, which is a gap in our knowledge, not a lack of explanation.}
\cpara{Concludes that a reducible brain can never get Bayesian confirmation for irreducibility.}

\clogic{The author conceded an objection to this passage in ``Psychic Powers,'' posted the same day. That post quotes it, answers Benja Fallenstein's objection with ``You're right,'' and adds a flaw of the author's own finding. An outcome that a reducible model could also produce can still make irreducibility much more probable, if the irreducible model produces it more simply. Fallenstein's example, a hypercomputer, also bears on the analogy in the next paragraph.}
\cpara{Gives an analogy from computability: in a Turing-computable universe we could not predict a halting oracle's answers well enough to tell it from computable reasoning.}
\cpara{Adds that all this assumes the usual view: to the extent you believe reductionism, you should expect non-reductionism to be incoherent as well as wrong.}
\cpara{Grants, with ``presumably,'' that a true supernatural hypothesis would turn out to be conceivable.}
\cpara{Returns to Intelligent Design.}
\cpara{Restates the opening question.}

\cpara{The answer: the designer's irreducibility is not needed, since every supernatural model has a reducible counterpart with the same predictions. ``Psychic Powers'' keeps this claim while conceding the one about confirmation.}

\cpara{Gives the Red Sea as a supernatural claim tested and failed. The historical point was checked in the notes on ``Religion's Claim to be Non-Disprovable'': scholars do not take the Exodus account as accurate, and Egypt did rule Canaan in the late second millennium BCE.}
\cpara{Adds evidence from biology against a benevolent designer, predators and prey designed against each other and the backward retina, both set out in ``An Alien God.''}
\cpara{States the method: convert the supernatural hypothesis into a natural one, derive or look up its predictions, and test them. A failed test excludes the claim a posteriori.}
\cpara{Defines reductionism as disbelief in ``fundamentally complicated'' things, and calls non-reductionism a confusion, with ``I think.''}
\cpara{Ends the argument: the rule of science is to look and see.}

\cpara{Adds a corollary: a designer of artificial general intelligence who speaks of religious beliefs respectfully is ignorant of the basics, a complete idiot savant, or lying. No designer is named.}

\clogic{The phrase links to ``Outside the Laboratory,'' which gives its sense: religious claims treated as open. The corollary then judges the expertise of unnamed designers from that one attitude, and allows only ignorance, ``idiot savancy'' or lying as explanations. No case is given.}
